jcr:content.jcr:title: Learn AEM
jcr:content.jcr:description: Your hands-on guide to Adobe Experience Manager. Explore templates, components, Sling Models, content architecture, and AEM as a Cloud Service best practices.

hero.title: Build enterprise websites with Adobe Experience Manager.
hero.description: AEM is the industry-leading content management platform used by Fortune 500 companies worldwide. This learning hub walks you through the architecture, components, templates, and best practices you need to build production-grade AEM sites from scratch.
hero.panelTitle: This site is a live AEM project
hero.panelText: Everything you see here runs on a real AEM instance. Custom components, editable templates, Sling Models, and SCSS styling — all following AEMaaCS best practices.

concepts_text.text: Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) is built on a powerful open-source stack: Apache Sling for RESTful content resolution, Apache Jackrabbit Oak (JCR) for hierarchical content storage, and OSGi for modular Java services. Understanding this foundation is key to building scalable AEM solutions.

item0.title: Editable Templates
item0.description: Templates define page structure and allowed components. AEM's editable templates let authors control layout policies, initial content, and component permissions — all without developer involvement.

item1.title: Components & HTL
item1.description: Components are the building blocks of AEM pages. Written in HTL (Sightly), they combine server-side rendering with a clean separation of markup, logic, and styling using BEM conventions.

item2.title: Sling Models
item2.description: Sling Models provide the Java backend for components. They inject JCR properties, traverse content trees, and expose business logic to HTL — all with simple annotations and pure Sling APIs.

item3.title: Content Architecture
item3.description: AEM uses a hierarchical content repository (JCR). Pages, assets, configurations, and templates are all resources in a tree structure that Sling resolves via resource types.

item4.title: Core Components
item4.description: Adobe's Core Components are a set of standardized, production-ready WCM components for AEM. They accelerate development, reduce maintenance costs, and follow accessibility best practices out of the box.

item5.title: Content Fragments
item5.description: Content Fragments let you create structured, channel-neutral content that can be delivered headlessly via GraphQL or embedded in AEM pages. Ideal for omnichannel content strategies.

item6.title: Experience Fragments
item6.description: Experience Fragments are reusable groups of components including content and layout. Use them for headers, footers, and promotional sections that appear across multiple pages.

item7.title: Dispatcher Caching
item7.description: The Dispatcher is AEM's caching and load-balancing layer. Proper configuration ensures fast page delivery, efficient cache invalidation, and secure content filtering at the edge.

item8.title: OSGi Configuration
item8.description: AEM runs on an OSGi container where services are modular and configurable. Manage run-mode specific configs for author, publish, dev, stage, and production environments.

tutorials_text.text: Each tutorial on this site is built as a real AEM page using the same components and patterns you would use in production. Explore the articles below to dive into specific topics, from getting started with AEM to advanced dispatcher caching strategies.

architecture_text.text:
A well-structured AEM project follows the Adobe AEM Project Archetype layout with clearly separated modules:

  • core/ — Java backend: Sling Models, OSGi services, servlets, and workflow steps
  • ui.apps/ — AEM components: HTL templates, dialogs (Coral UI), and client libraries
  • ui.content/ — Content packages: templates, policies, and authored pages
  • ui.frontend/ — Frontend build: SCSS, JavaScript, and Webpack bundling
  • ui.config/ — OSGi configurations for run modes (author, publish, dev, stage, prod)
  • dispatcher/ — Apache/Dispatcher rules for caching, rewrites, and security filters

This separation ensures clean deployments, testable code, and a clear boundary between content and application logic.

bestpractices_text.text:
Following proven patterns makes your AEM projects maintainable, performant, and ready for AEM as a Cloud Service:

  • Use Core Components — Extend Adobe's Core Components instead of building from scratch. They are tested, accessible, and continuously updated.
  • Pure Sling APIs — Avoid com.day.cq.wcm.api in Sling Models. Use Resource, ValueMap, and ResourceResolver for SDK compatibility.
  • Editable Templates — Use editable templates with policies over static templates. They give authors more control and reduce developer bottlenecks.
  • Content Fragments & Experience Fragments — Model structured content with Content Fragments for omnichannel delivery. Use Experience Fragments for reusable page sections.
  • Dispatcher Caching — Configure dispatcher rules to cache aggressively, invalidate precisely, and serve stale content during revalidation.
  • CI/CD with Cloud Manager — Use Cloud Manager pipelines for automated builds, code quality gates, and staged deployments.

cloudservice_text.text:
AEM as a Cloud Service (AEMaaCS) is the cloud-native evolution of AEM. It introduces auto-scaling, continuous delivery via Cloud Manager, and a microservices architecture for asset processing. Key differences from AEM 6.5 include:

  • Immutable repository — The /apps and /libs paths are read-only at runtime. All code deploys through CI/CD pipelines.
  • No JMX or CRXDE on prod — Debugging relies on logs, Developer Console, and health checks.
  • Asset microservices — Rendition generation, metadata extraction, and PDF processing are handled by cloud-native workers instead of local AEM workflows.
  • Rapid Development Environments (RDE) — Lightweight cloud environments for quick iteration without full pipeline deployments.

Building with AEMaaCS best practices from day one — as this project does — ensures a smooth path to production.
